certainty_reasoning: The longest documented relationship of Ross's life - roughly a decade, 1903 to autumn 1913 - and the fullest treatment of it is Fryer's, in his own narrating voice. Fryer states the relationship plainly and repeatedly rather than hedging it, so the class reflects who is talking, not any doubt that it happened. Margery Ross, Friend of Friends (1952), is Fryer's main source for Ross's own voice and is the place to look for first-hand material.
summary: Ross met Smith early in 1903, when Smith was an eighteen-year-old clerk. Smith became his secretary - a post that doubled as cover - and moved into 15 Vicarage Gardens in 1906 despite his family's objections. The relationship lasted about a decade, ending in the autumn of 1913, months before Douglas named Smith in the 1914 plea of justification.

sources.quote: And early in 1903, he met a young man with whom he entered into a relationship quite unlike his other brief encounters with boys. Frederick (Freddie) Smith was an attractive, unpretentious, eighteen-year-old clerk; not someone of Robbie's class or intellectual capacity, but nonetheless keen to learn and improve himself.
sources.context: Fryer opening the Freddie Smith thread. He continues on the same page: 'The fact that Robbie was almost twice his age does not seem to have particularly bothered either of them'. Ages stated exactly as Fryer states them (readme register rule).
sources.supports: Start of the relationship, the ages, and Fryer's framing of it as unlike Ross's other encounters.
sources.provenance: PDF page 199 of Fryer_2000_Robbie-Ross, printed folio 177 confirmed on the rendered page. Offset is +22 in this half of the scan.

sources.quote: Astonishingly, Robbie reacted to this latest example of Edwardian England's homophobia by defiantly inviting his young secretary-companion Freddie Smith to move in with him in a charming house, on which he had taken a short lease, at 15 Vicarage Gardens, Kensington, just a few minutes walk from his previous rooms in Hornton Street.
sources.context: 1906, in the paragraph immediately after Christopher Millard's arrest and three-month sentence for gross indecency. The next sentences record the family's horror and their deputing of Ross's nephew Edward Jones to remonstrate.
sources.supports: Documented cohabitation, and the pivot out of the Adey household into a household with Smith.
sources.provenance: PDF page 214, printed folio 192 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Though he never flaunted his homosexuality in public, Robbie saw no reason to be ashamed of his relationship with Freddie, who had not yet turned twenty. Moreover, he was becoming increasingly proud of his young protege, who had developed into a talented amateur actor. He used his second name Stanley on stage. Shamelessly, Robbie took advantage of his journalistic outlets to promote his lover's acting career
sources.context: C. 1906. Ross's own Academy review of Smith's performance is block-quoted on the same page ('rendered with marvellous skill by Mr F. Stanley Smith').
sources.supports: Fryer's flat use of 'his lover' for Smith; the age; and Ross's public unashamedness about the relationship.
sources.provenance: PDF page 215, printed folio 193 confirmed on the rendered page. The quotation stops at a clause boundary without elision marks because the remainder of the sentence names the play reviewed; no words are dropped from within the quoted span.

sources.quote: On the home front, he had decided to terminate his relationship with Freddie Smith, who had failed to give him the sort of loving support he had needed during his recent troubles. Although he knew Freddie would feign enthusiasm at his return, he was conscious that the passion had gone out of their union, and that more disappointment and heartache would lie ahead if he did not bring things to an end.
sources.context: Autumn 1913, on Ross's journey home from Russia, reaching London on 5 October, amid the threat of action by Douglas and Crosland.
sources.supports: End of the relationship, and its decade-long span (early 1903 to autumn 1913).
sources.provenance: PDF page 252, printed folio 230 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Thirteen other witnesses were produced in Bosie's defence, including a young woman who had taken part in amateur dramatics with Freddie Smith. She testified that she had seen Robbie hug Freddie and call him 'my darling'. A priest, whom Freddie had served as an acolyte, spoke of his revulsion when he had seen Robbie's lover with make-up on his face.
sources.context: Ross's prosecution of Douglas for criminal libel, Old Bailey, opened 19 November 1914. Douglas's plea of justification (p. 237) cited 'four cases of alleged gross indecency: with Biscoe Wortham's Bruges pupil, Dansey, two decades before, Freddie Smith, Charlie Garratt and a boy called William Edwards.' H. G. Wells testified for the prosecution that he had met Smith several times at Ross's home 'and never noticed anything of the sort'.
sources.supports: The third-party attestation of the Ross-Smith relationship that survives is sworn testimony gathered by a hostile ex-friend for a prosecution - the evidentiary shape the revised taxonomy exists to record.
sources.provenance: PDF page 260, printed folio 238 confirmed on the rendered page; the plea-of-justification sentence quoted in the context line was verified at PDF page 259, printed folio 237.
